title: 2026 budget review: 2.2% property tax increase
subtitle: Library lockers, $1 million strategic fund, user fees, golf dividends, Centre in the Square, traffic calming
overview: The Finance and Corporate Services Committee spent the day reviewing the proposed 2026 operating and capital budgets, titled "Affordable Today and Ready for Tomorrow". Staff proposed a 2.2% property tax increase, about $29 for the average household. With a 6.3% water utilities increase (about $88), the combined impact is about $117 a year, or under $10 a month. The 10-year capital forecast covers more than 400 projects totalling $1.8 billion.

The minutes provided record no motions or votes for this meeting, so the committee made no recommendations to Council. Members heard from Centre in the Square and the Kitchener Public Library, reviewed tax-supported and enterprise budgets, user fees, debt, reserves and development charges, and discussed how to use $1 million of one-time strategic funding.

This was the feedback step before the Mayor formally tables the budget on December 1, 2025. Final budget day is December 11, 2025. Residents can expect any changes to be made then. The City says its portion is about 30% of the total property tax bill. The Region and school boards make up the rest.
debate: Library lockers: several members supported adding lockers, with Kingsdale and Centreville Chicopee named. Staff said funding could go to the library, but the library board would decide how to use it and would need to confirm it could staff more lockers. The library wanted to pilot one more year.

Use of the $1 million strategic fund: members leaned toward park amenities such as seating, shade and playgrounds, and special event equipment such as a big screen. Some also backed business retention and Kitchener Pitch. One councillor cautioned that cricket demand could fall, while others said cricket facilities could be converted to other sports.

User fees: some members worried that new public tree removal and development review fees could discourage infill and affordable housing. Staff said the tree fees follow the public tree by-law, are based on industry standards, and large tree fees would be rare on boulevards. Several members asked for further discussion.

Golf and finances: some councillors wanted a golf dividend to return. Staff said there are no retained earnings yet, since the golf stabilization fund is projected to stay in deficit. They also said City debt cannot be paid off early once issued.

Traffic calming and other requests: several councillors pressed to expand the flexi-sign program in 2026. Staff said it would need more installation staff and that provincial funding may help. Members also raised temporary washrooms at McLennan Park and asked whether the budget funds a possible renoviction by-law, which staff said it does not yet.
